section_summary: This section covers the turbulent period in Japanese domestic politics from December 1931 through June 1932, documenting the fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and the installation of the Seiyukai government under Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai. It details the February 1932 general elections in which the Seiyukai won a commanding majority, the subsequent assassination of Prime Minister Inukai by young naval and army officers in the May 15 Incident, and the ensuing collapse of party-led cabinets. Diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and State Department memoranda chronicle the formation of a national unity compromise government under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito, assessing its cabinet roster, the dominant influence of War Minister Sadao Araki and military factions, and looming crises involving agrarian unrest, zaibatsu dominance, economic depression, and the recognition of Manchukuo.

subfiles.about: Concluding fragment of a diplomatic document discussing the political advantages gained by opponents from the embarrassment of the government party.
subfiles.summary: This single-sentence fragment concludes a discussion on Japanese domestic politics. It observes that opposition elements stand to gain from the embarrassment of the government party.
subfiles.title: Fragment on Japanese Party Politics

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a Far Eastern Division memorandum regarding persistent rumors of the Wakatsuki Cabinet's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a State Department Far Eastern Division memorandum dated December 11, 1931, prepared by Miller. The memorandum outlines the reasons behind persistent rumors concerning the resignation of Prime Minister Wakatsuki's Cabinet. It also offers predictions on who would be called to form the successor government and from which party it would be drawn.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/335

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a London embassy despatch commenting on Japanese Cabinet changes and enclosing a Times editorial.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 2495 forwarded from London by Ray Atherton on December 18, 1931. The despatch comments on the recent collapse and reconfiguration of the Japanese Cabinet. It encloses an editorial from The Times of London dated December 14, 1931, reviewing the political transition.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 2495 (894.002/172)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 422 analyzing the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and attendant political developments.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 422 sent by Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes from Tokyo on December 17, 1931. It provides an extensive discussion and commentary on the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet. The despatch analyzes the political maneuvers leading up to the fall and the immediate consequences for Japanese governance.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 422 (894.002/173)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a Military Intelligence Division report on the Home Minister's advocacy for a national coalition government.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Military Intelligence Division Report No. 5985 dated December 3, 1931, prepared by the U.S. Military Attaché in Japan. It reviews the worsening Cabinet situation in Tokyo. It highlights that the Minister of Home Affairs is advocating for a National Government to resolve national difficulties.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: M.I.D. Report No. 5985 (894.002/174)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 460 reporting on the assassination attempt against Emperor Hirohito and the Cabinet's response.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 460 sent by Ambassador Forbes on January 16, 1932. It addresses the Sakuradamon incident, an assassination attempt against the Emperor of Japan by Korean activist Li Ho-sho (Shoichi Asayama). It also details observations on the incident and the subsequent political course taken by the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 460 (894.002/175)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 458 listing the ministerial appointments of the new Inukai Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 458 (Political Report No. 49) forwarded by Ambassador Forbes on January 15, 1932. It records the Cabinet changes in Japan following the fall of the previous ministry. A complete roster of ministers installed under Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai on December 13, 1931, is indexed.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 458 (894.002/176)

subfiles.about: Extract from Despatch No. 458 presenting the ministerial roster of the Inukai Cabinet and recounting the political intrigues that ended the Wakatsuki government.
subfiles.summary: This extract details the formal installation of the Seiyukai Cabinet under Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai on December 13, 1931, listing every cabinet minister and portfolio. It identifies Home Minister Kenzo Adachi's persistent intrigue for a coalition government as the immediate cause of the deadlock that forced Premier Wakatsuki's resignation. It notes that the Japanese public exhibited little enthusiasm for the Seiyukai's return to power due to memories of past corruption, while referencing alleged Mitsui financial influence in the government's downfall.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 458 (Extract): Installation of the Inukai Cabinet and Political Background

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 471 reporting the dissolution of the Diet and scheduling of a general election for February 20, 1932.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 471 from Ambassador Forbes in Tokyo, dated January 29, 1932. It records that following the dissolution of the Diet, an extraordinary meeting of the Cabinet set February 20 as the date for general elections.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 471 (894.002/177)

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting on the dissolution of the 60th Diet and analyzing party platforms, issues, and prospects for the February 1932 election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that the 60th Diet was dissolved by Imperial Ordinance on January 21, 1932, and the Inukai Cabinet scheduled general elections for February 20. The Government dissolved the Lower House immediately after opening speeches to preempt the Minseito majority from mounting an attack over the Sakuradamon incident. The despatch contrasts the party platforms: the Seiyukai advocates bond financing, a five-year industrial plan, rice monopolies, suspension of the gold standard, and cooperation with the Army in Manchuria, while the Minseito supports deflation, the gold standard, and tax increases. Forbes predicts a Seiyukai victory due to government control over local election officials, extensive campaign funding from banking profits after the gold embargo, and Inukai's shrewd leadership.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 471: Dissolution of the Diet and the Forthcoming General Elections

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 509 reporting that the Seiyukai gained an absolute majority of 157 seats over the Minseito.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 509 dated February 27, 1932, from Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo. It summarizes election results showing that the ruling Seiyukai secured a 157-seat majority over the opposition Minseito in the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 509 (894.002/178)

subfiles.about: Exhaustive diplomatic despatch analyzing the results, structural causes, and systemic ramifications of the Seiyukai's landslide victory in the 1932 general election.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Neville provides an in-depth analysis of the February 20, 1932 general election, in which the ruling Seiyukai won a historic landslide of 304 seats while the Minseito plummeted to 147. The defeat of the Minseito is attributed to internal fractures following Hamaguchi's death, Adachi's defection, and the assassination of campaign manager Junnosuke Inouye just prior to voting, alongside widespread public rejection of deflationary retrenchment. The Seiyukai benefited decisively from official control over prefectural governors and police, generous campaign funds from financial firms benefiting from the reimposed gold embargo, and public rally-around-the-flag sentiment regarding military actions in China. The report examines the declining influence of proletarian parties, growing popular cynicism toward parliamentarism and fears of fascism, and noteworthy individual contests, including the election of the first Korean Diet member, Boku Shin Kin.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 509: Detailed Report on the Japanese General Election of February 20, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Ambassador Forbes's report transmitting the Navy Minister's address at a farewell luncheon given in his honor.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a report from Tokyo dated March 19, 1932, submitted by Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes. It concerns a farewell luncheon hosted by the Japanese Minister of Marine in honor of Forbes and transmits the text of the Minister's speech.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Farewell Luncheon for Ambassador Forbes (894.002/179)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Forbes transmits personal impressions of easing political tensions in Tokyo and encloses an address delivered by Navy Minister Osumi praising Japanese-American naval ties.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes writes confidentially to Secretary Stimson that political tension in Tokyo has eased noticeably, citing reports from European diplomats and journalists. He describes interactions with Japanese military leaders, remarking on the cordiality of War Minister Sadao Araki and Admiral Toyoda compared to the evasiveness of retired General Sato. Forbes encloses the formal address delivered by Minister of the Navy Admiral Mineo Osumi at a farewell luncheon on March 18, 1932. Osumi's speech commends Forbes for easing international misunderstandings surrounding Manchuria and Shanghai and stresses the importance of naval friendship as an anchor of peace.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Forbes to Secretary of State Stimson Transmitting Address by Admiral Mineo Osumi

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 126 reporting the shooting and critical wounding of Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 126 sent from Tokyo by Chargé Neville on May 15, 1932. It records the violent attack on Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai, who was shot and critically wounded by uniformed attackers.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 126 (894.002/180)

subfiles.about: Immediate diplomatic report on the shooting of Prime Minister Inukai, attacks on Count Makino's residence, and bombings by uniformed young officers.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville transmits breaking information received orally from the Japanese Foreign Office that Prime Minister Inukai was shot and left in critical condition on the evening of May 15, 1932. Uniformed military and naval assailants riding in automobiles also assaulted Count Makino's residence, fired shots at the Metropolitan Police Department resulting in a fatality, and bombed Seiyukai headquarters. Neville reports that eighteen attackers belonging to a young officers' association opposing corruption and capitalism surrendered or were arrested. The rest of the city remained calm, with no anti-foreign manifestations or danger to Americans.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 126: Armed Attacks on Prime Minister Inukai and Government Offices in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 128 reporting the resignation of the Cabinet following Prime Minister Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 128 dated May 16, 1932, from Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo. It records the formal resignation of the Cabinet following the death of Prime Minister Inukai from gunshot wounds.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 128 (894.002/181)

subfiles.about: Telegram confirming the formal resignation of the Cabinet following Premier Inukai's death and noting outward calm in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville reports that the State Department's instructions in Telegram No. 106 have been executed. He advises that the Japanese Cabinet has just submitted its resignation following the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai. The capital remains outwardly calm while political leaders assess the crisis.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 128: Resignation of the Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 560 explaining that Home Minister Nakahashi resigned due to moral responsibility for the Sakuradamon incident.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 560 (Political Report No. 52) from Chargé Neville, dated April 7, 1932. It clarifies that Tokugoro Nakahashi's resignation as Minister of Home Affairs stemmed from traditional Japanese notions of responsibility for the January assassination attempt against the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 560 (894.002/182)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 136 reporting delays in announcing the personnel of the new Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 136 sent by Edwin L. Neville on May 23, 1932. It notes that the announcement of personnel for the newly mandated Cabinet had not yet been made and was unlikely for several days.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 136 (894.002/183)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito was commanded by the Emperor to form a compromise national government.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville informs the Secretary of State that Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito received an Imperial command on May 22 to form a Cabinet. Saito's designation represents a compromise between extreme nationalism and party politics, proving acceptable to the military, political parties, and the public. Although the press laments the break from party cabinet conventions, it considers the step necessary under prevailing emergency conditions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 136: Viscount Saito Commanded to Form Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 580 on the death sentence handed down to Hamaguchi's assassin, Tomeo Sagoya.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 580 (Political Report No. 53) dated May 5, 1932, from Chargé Neville. It reports that the Tokyo District Court sentenced Tomeo Sagoya to death for fatally shooting former Prime Minister Hamaguchi.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 580 (894.002/184)

subfiles.about: Extract from Despatch No. 580 reporting the death sentence imposed on Hamaguchi's assassin and the departure of Dr. Inazo Nitobe for the United States.
subfiles.summary: This extract reports that the Tokyo District Court sentenced Tomeo Sagoya to death for the fatal shooting of ex-Premier Hamaguchi, noting that the severity of the sentence reflected official alarm over recent terrorism by secret societies. The document also records the departure of Dr. and Mrs. Inazo Nitobe on April 14 for a good-will tour of the United States.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 580 (Extract): Death Sentence for Tomeo Sagoya and Departure of Dr. Nitobe

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 141 reporting the formal installation of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 141 from Chargé Neville in Tokyo, dated May 26, 1932. It records the installation of the new Cabinet and notes that Viscount Saito will temporarily serve as Foreign Minister alongside the premiership.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 141 (894.002/185)

subfiles.about: Telegram announcing the installation of the Saito Cabinet, its bipartisan and non-party composition, and plans to convene the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville reports that the new Cabinet was installed on the afternoon of May 26, 1932, with Viscount Makoto Saito temporarily holding the foreign affairs portfolio in addition to the premiership. The Diet is expected to convene the following week to receive government proposals for dealing with the national crisis. The Cabinet includes representatives of both the Seiyukai and Minseito parties as well as non-partisan figures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 141: Formal Installation of the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 571 from Peiping relaying reports on the roster and reception of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 571 sent from Peiping by Minister Nelson T. Johnson on May 27, 1932. It summarizes news reports on the formation and roster of Viscount Saito's Cabinet and provides estimates of public, financial, and military reactions.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 571 (894.002/186)

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting Nippon Dempo reporting on the newly formed Saito Cabinet, internal party rivalries, and public and financial disappointment.
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson forwards dispatches from the Nippon Dempo news agency reciting the ministerial appointments in the newly formed Saito administration. Japanese commentary reflects widespread public and financial skepticism, characterizing the ministry as a collection of second-class figures lacking cohesion. Press reports anticipate friction between Home Minister Yamamoto (Minseito) and Finance Minister Takahashi (Seiyukai), as well as between ministerial sub-factions. While military circles did not obtain the full coalition they sought, they accept the arrangement as a satisfactory transitional, non-party government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 571: Nippon Dempo Reports on the Saito Cabinet Roster and Factional Doubts

subfiles.about: Secretary Stimson records discussions with Ambassador Debuchi regarding the Saito Cabinet, General Araki's role, prospective foreign ministers, and railway rumors.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson summarizes a conversation with Japanese Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi regarding the newly formed Saito government. Debuchi expressed satisfaction that General Araki remained as War Minister, believing he could be better monitored within the cabinet, and praised Admiral Saito's liberal and steady character. The diplomats reviewed prospective candidates for the foreign affairs portfolio, including SMR President Uchida and London Ambassador Matsudaira. Debuchi also firmly denied press rumors regarding Japanese negotiations in Paris to purchase the Chinese Eastern Railway.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Secretary of State Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Minister Johnson in Peiping a copy of Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Stimson forwards Instruction No. 774 to American Minister Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping, enclosing a strictly confidential copy of his May 26 memorandum of conversation with Ambassador Debuchi concerning the Saito Cabinet. The text is restricted to Johnson's personal use, with authorization to share it at his discretion with legation counselors.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 774 to Nelson T. Johnson Enclosing Memorandum of May 26, 1932

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Chargé Neville in Tokyo a copy of Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Stimson transmits Instruction No. 336 to Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo, providing a strictly confidential copy of his May 26 memorandum of conversation with Ambassador Debuchi regarding the Saito Cabinet. The document is designated exclusively for Neville's personal information and not for general embassy distribution.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 336 to Edwin L. Neville Enclosing Memorandum of May 26, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 572 reporting colonial and military command changes resulting from the Saito Cabinet's formation.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 572 sent by Nelson T. Johnson from Peiping on May 27, 1932. It records the appointment of Count Kodama as Governor General of Formosa and Lieutenant General Kawashima as Commander-in-Chief in Korea to replace officials joining the Saito Cabinet. It also reviews the political outlook confronting the new government.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 572 (894.002/188)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 148 advising on the availability of Prime Minister Saito's Diet speeches.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 148 sent by Edwin L. Neville from Tokyo on June 3, 1932. It notes that the full texts of Prime Minister Saito's policy speeches before the Imperial Diet can be obtained from the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 148 (894.002/189)

subfiles.about: Under Secretary Castle records Ambassador Debuchi's detailed personal assessments of the ministers comprising the new Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary William R. Castle, Jr. records an extensive interview with Japanese Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi regarding the composition of the Saito ministry. Debuchi characterized the government as refreshingly liberal, arguing that keeping General Araki in the War Ministry ensures greater accountability and praising Navy Minister Okada for his moderation. He offered favorable appraisals of Home Minister Yamamoto, Overseas Minister Nagai, Commerce Minister Nakajima, Railway Minister Mitsuchi, Justice Minister Koyama, Agriculture Minister Goto, and Finance Minister Takahashi, highlighting their professional backgrounds and moderate tendencies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Under Secretary Castle and Ambassador Debuchi

subfiles.about: Confidential instruction transmitting to Chargé Neville in Tokyo a copy of Under Secretary Castle's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary Castle, writing on behalf of the Secretary of State, forwards Instruction No. 331 to Chargé Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo. The instruction encloses for staff use a confidential copy of Castle's May 26 memorandum recording Ambassador Debuchi's evaluations of the members of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 331 to Edwin L. Neville Enclosing Memorandum of May 26, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 650 reporting Count Uchida's prospective meeting with Premier Saito regarding the foreign affairs portfolio.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 650 sent from Peiping by Nelson T. Johnson on June 14, 1932. It records that SMR President Count Yasuya Uchida was scheduled to confer with Viscount Saito regarding an offer to become Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 650 (894.002/191)

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting Reuter reports on joint party moves to recognize Manchukuo and Count Uchida's consultations regarding the foreign affairs portfolio.
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits Reuter reports from Tokyo detailing plans by both the Minseito and Seiyukai to introduce joint Diet resolutions demanding immediate recognition of Manchukuo. Count Yasuya Uchida held conferences with War Minister Araki concerning Manchurian policy prior to an anticipated meeting with Premier Saito regarding the Foreign Ministry. Although the Cabinet is sympathetic to recognition, official sources indicate formal action may be postponed until the Lytton Commission submits its findings in September.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 650: Reuter Reports on Manchukuo Recognition and Count Uchida's Deliberations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 654 reporting the imminent installation of Count Uchida as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 654 from Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping, dated June 15, 1932. It indicates that Count Yasuya Uchida would likely be installed as Minister for Foreign Affairs following a final conference with Premier Saito.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 654 (894.002/192)

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting news reports on policy agreements reached between Count Uchida and General Araki regarding Manchukuo and Uchida's acceptance of the Foreign portfolio.
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits a Nippon Dempo account of a pivotal conference between Count Yasuya Uchida and War Minister Sadao Araki on June 14, 1932. The two leaders agreed that formal recognition of Manchukuo should occur as soon as treaty adjustments are prepared, that Japanese administrative power in Manchuria should unify under the Kwantung Army commander, and that the SMR should transition into a strictly commercial enterprise. Having secured Araki's support to retain the SMR presidency concurrently, Uchida agreed to accept the post of Foreign Minister under Premier Saito following the upcoming shareholders' meeting in Dairen.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 654: Nippon Dempo Report on Uchida-Araki Accord on Manchukuo and Foreign Ministry

subfiles.about: State Department analysis summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 635 on the composition of the Saito Cabinet and five urgent foreign and domestic challenges.
subfiles.summary: This State Department Far Eastern Division memorandum summarizes Despatch No. 635 from Tokyo analyzing the newly formed Saito administration. It characterizes the ministry as an effective super-party cabinet dominated by War Minister Araki and the young military faction, supported by four senior statesmen—Saito, Araki, Takahashi, and Yamamoto—and eight mediocre members. The analysis outlines five critical problems confronting the government: severe agrarian and social unrest fueled by hatred of zaibatsu monopolies (Mitsui, Iwasaki, Sumitomo); massive fiscal deficits necessitating loans and inflation; public disillusionment with party politics; the looming international crisis over the League of Nations commission report on Manchuria; and strained relations with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Despatch No. 635: The Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting on the formation, personnel, factional balance, public reactions, and challenges of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville provides an extensive examination of the newly installed Cabinet formed under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito following the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai by young officers. The despatch explains that the administration represents an uneasy compromise between military radicals demanding an end to party politics and Prince Saionji's defense of constitutionalism. Neville provides biographical and political analyses of all twelve ministers, identifying Saito, War Minister Araki, Finance Minister Takahashi, and Home Minister Yamamoto as the only leaders of high caliber, while noting that Araki effectively dominates policy. Public, political, and financial circles are described as disappointed by the ministry's mediocre composition, as it faces unprecedented domestic crises of agrarian distress, debt, and zaibatsu resentment alongside international tensions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 635: The Saito Cabinet
